analysis.one_liner: Bans for-profit corporations from running political action committees.
analysis.headline: The Senate referred the Ban Corporate PACs Act to committee on January 20, 2022, and it never received a hearing, vote, or action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend federal election law so that only nonprofit corporations can create and operate separate segregated funds — the corporate PACs that companies use to pool donations from employees and give to candidates. For-profit corporations would be barred from establishing new corporate PACs, and existing ones would have to terminate and disburse their balances within one year of enactment. The bill would also narrow solicitation to executive and administrative personnel only, removing shareholders from the pool of people a corporate PAC can ask for money, and would apply the same limits to government contractors. It received no committee action, no vote, and died when the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: The main beneficiaries would be candidates and voters who want to reduce the flow of corporate money into federal campaigns: candidates would no longer receive bundled corporate PAC checks, and political parties/candidates would have to rely more on small-dollar donations, individual giving, and other funding channels. Nonprofit organizations' PACs would be relatively advantaged over for-profit corporate PACs.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters and candidates seeking less corporate money

how_it_helps.text: Bars for-profit corporations from establishing or operating corporate PACs, cutting off a major channel of bundled corporate money to congressional campaigns.
Restricts corporate PAC solicitation to executive and administrative personnel, ending the practice of soliciting shareholders and their families.
Requires existing corporate PACs to terminate and disburse their balances within one year, rather than letting them wind down indefinitely.

analysis.who_pays: For-profit corporations and their government affairs operations would lose their main PAC vehicle for organizing and delivering campaign contributions to federal candidates; trade associations and business PAC infrastructure would lose a source of funding and a channel for political access. Corporate PAC contributions currently go to both parties, so members of both parties who rely on this money would be affected.
analysis.who_pays_short: Corporate PACs and their business sponsors

drawbacks.text: Critics note that corporate PACs are one of the most transparent forms of political spending, with names and amounts disclosed; banning them may push corporate political activity toward harder-to-trace channels like super PACs and dark-money groups, which are less accountable than the PACs being banned.

Candidates and parties of both parties rely on corporate PAC money for campaign operations; removing it shifts fundraising burdens toward other channels without addressing other forms of corporate influence.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a specific, well-litigated, transparent channel of corporate money. Its benefit — removing corporate PAC checks from federal campaigns — is real but limited: corporate political influence has many other channels. Its main cost is that it may displace corporate political spending into less transparent forms. Honest supporters and critics agree it is a partial measure, not a fix for money in politics generally.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in the Senate and referred to the Rules and Administration Committee, where it stayed without a hearing or vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced in the Senate on January 20, 2022, by Sen. Mark Kelly with Sen. Jon Ossoff.
Referred to the Senate Committee on Rules and Administration the same day.
No further action was taken; the bill never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Corporate PACs and the business and political interests that rely on corporate PAC contributions were better off, because the ban never advanced beyond introduction. The committee never acted, and no vote was ever scheduled, so the status quo of corporate PAC fundraising was preserved for the remainder of the 117th Congress.

for.name: Sen. Mark Kelly
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to committee.

for.name: Sen. Jon Ossoff
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill as an original cosponsor at introduction.

against.name: Senate Rules and Administration Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the remainder of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had only two Democratic sponsors and never reached a vote, so no roll-call record shows how the parties would have split; corporate PAC money flows to members of both parties, and no public chamber division is on the record here.

industries.note: Corporate PACs are a mechanism for businesses to organize and deliver bundled campaign contributions to federal candidates. A ban eliminates that tool, which is why business-oriented groups have historically opposed similar proposals in other bills (not on the record here).
The bill explicitly permits nonprofit corporations (501(c) organizations) to keep or establish PACs, giving nonprofits a relative advantage over for-profit corporate PACs.
The bill applies the same ban to corporations with federal government contracts, removing their corporate PAC vehicle for contributing to campaigns.
